The Problem with Habits

PEOPLE DON'T
QUIT HABITS.
THEY QUIT WAITING
FOR THE PAYOFF.

Most habit apps track streaks and call it motivation. But a streak is just a number — it doesn't feel like anything. Habit 21 is my attempt to fix that: a 21-day habit-building app built around one idea — the reward has to be real, and it has to be yours.

See the case study → View screens
Problem → evidence → decision → outcome

The project changed when I stopped treating a streak as the reward.

Problem

Habit apps counted consistency but made one missed day feel like failure. The experience created pressure without giving users a meaningful reason to return.

Evidence

Interviews and small studies pointed to the same friction: people did not always quit because the habit was difficult; they quit when the effort felt emotionally empty.

Direction explored

I compared generic badges, streak protection and social accountability. Each added motivation, but none preserved ownership as clearly as a self-chosen real reward.

Trade-off

A strict 21-day journey creates focus, but it can become punitive. I balanced structure with reflection, visible progress and positive milestones instead of shame-driven resets.

Solution

Users choose a reward on Day 1, check in once a day and see the payoff move closer. Every screen reinforces anticipation, momentum and personal commitment.

Outcome + reflection

The concept became an end-to-end clickable system spanning 837+ screens. Next, I would compare completion and return rates against a conventional streak-only version.

Problem Statement

WHAT'S ACTUALLY
BROKEN ABOUT
HABIT APPS?

Most habit-tracking apps focus on streaks as the primary motivator. Streaks alone don't sustain motivation past the first week — they create pressure without payoff.

The core gap: there's nothing to look forward to. When a streak breaks, shame replaces momentum.

Habit 21 fixes this. The reward isn't a badge inside the app — it's something real, chosen by you, waiting on Day 21.

No payoff
Streaks count what you've done but give nothing back. Without a reward to anticipate, motivation fades fast.
Shame after missing
One missed day feels like failure. Streak resets punish rather than support.
Gamification without meaning
Generic badges feel arbitrary. They're not tied to anything the user actually values.
The fix
Set a personal reward on Day 1. Check in for 21 days. Earn it on Day 21.
Research

I DIDN'T GUESS
AT THIS —
I TESTED IT

Before designing a single screen, I wanted to understand why habits fail, not just that they do. I ran small studies and interviews with people building daily habits — journaling, workouts, reading.

People didn't quit because the habit was hard. They quit because there was nothing to look forward to.

Rewards you choose for yourself motivate more consistently — they preserve ownership over the habit rather than turning it into a task someone else is grading.

"A streak tells you what you did. A reward tells you it was worth it."

Core research insight — Habit 21
The Finding
People didn't quit because the habit was hard. They quit because there was nothing to look forward to.
The Psychology
Anticipation of a reward drives behavior more than the reward itself. Self-chosen rewards preserve ownership.
The Design Decision
The reward must be chosen before Day 1 — not as a celebration after, but as the commitment itself.
The Rule
The reward doesn't need to be big. It needs to be real, earned, and chosen by the person.

Logo & Identity

THE NUMBERS
WERE ALWAYS
THE POINT

The name "Habit 21" carries the whole mechanic — 21 couldn't just sit next to the wordmark. It had to live inside it.

The version that worked treats the 2 and 1 as shapes hidden in the negative space of the letterforms. The wordmark reads as one word first, then reveals the number on a second look — mirroring the product: you don't notice Day 21 coming until you're already there.

Final
Ha2bit® — the 2 lives inside the wordmark. Legible as one word, rewards a second look.
The Solution

SET IT ON DAY 1.
EARN IT ON DAY 21.

1
Choose a habit and set a personal reward
Decided upfront — not assigned, chosen by you.
2
Check in daily for 21 days
Write one short sentence. Small enough to never feel like a chore.
3
Complete Day 21 and claim your reward
The app treats this as a real moment. You set it. You earned it.
4
Unlock an exclusive offer
Tied to real things — a discount on something you'd actually do.
5
Continue or start a new habit
Each completed cycle builds momentum for the next.

→

"Habit + Reward = Completion." Set the reward first. Everything else follows.
The core insight behind every screen in Ha2bit — not a tagline, a design constraint.

Design Approach

WHERE CAN
I HELP YOU

Habit-forming UX
▾
Designing for behaviour change

Every screen was designed to reduce friction at the daily check-in. The 3-option check-in (Yes / Not Yet / Missed) is non-judgmental by design — no streak resets, no shame spirals.

Check-in flowStreak designNon-judgmental UX
Psychology-based Design
▾
Grounded in how people actually behave

Built on reward psychology: anticipation of a reward drives behaviour more than the reward itself. Setting it before Day 1 makes it a commitment — not an afterthought.

Reward anticipationBehaviour loopsSelf-determination theory
Reward System Architecture
▾
Layered rewards that feel earned

Three reward layers: the personal reward (chosen by the user), partner brand offers (Nike, Adidas — Day 21 only), and a certificate of completion. None of it feels like a badge you forgot you earned.

Personal rewardNike × Ha2bitAdidas × Ha2bit25 badge system
Design Systems & Components
▾
Consistent, scalable, intentional

6 colour tokens, 2-font type scale (DM Serif Display + DM Sans), reusable components for nav, cards, buttons, check-in states, and badge grids. Every screen uses the same visual language.

6 colour tokensType scaleComponent library
iOS App Design in Figma
▾
837+ screens across 7 complete flows

Designed at 430×932px (iOS standard) with a Whoop-inspired aesthetic for the streak dashboard. Bold stats on dark olive cards — because progress should feel significant, not gamified.

430×932px iOS837+ screens7 flowsWhoop aesthetic
User Research & Testing
▾
Research-first, not assumption-first

Three personas — Ambica, Lakshman, Saketh — each revealed the same root cause: not hard habits, but empty ones. No payoff. This shaped every design decision from onboarding to Day 21.

User interviews3 personasEmpathy mappingJourney mapping
Wireframing & Prototyping
▾
Paper → Digital → Hi-fi, in order

Crazy 8s to break assumptions, paper wireframes for structure, digital lo-fi before touching colour or type. Each phase had a clear job before moving on.

Crazy 8sPaper wireframesDigital lo-fiFigma prototypes
Visual Design & Branding
▾
A visual language that matches the feeling

Cream background, dark olive cards, burnt orange accents. Warm but deliberate. The Ha2bit® logo hides the "21" inside the wordmark — it reveals itself on a second look, just like Day 21 itself.

Colour systemDM Serif Display + DM SansLogo design
The Big Idea

REWARD THE
SMALL STUFF.
PEOPLE KEEP
GOING.

Habit 21 isn't trying to guilt anyone into consistency. People stick with things when there's something real waiting for them at the end, chosen by them.

Every part of the app — the check-in, the streak, the Day 21 moment, the offer — exists to make that payoff feel real instead of decorative.

Core Insight
"Habit + Reward = Completion." Set the reward first. Everything else follows.
